card.chief_complaint: fever and mild cough after knee replacement

ask.changes_what: Shaking chills should prompt blood cultures and a search for a bacteremic source (line, biliary, urinary, endovascular); no chills supports withholding cultures when pretest probability is low.
ask.do_not_use_when: The RCE conclusions do not apply to immunocompromised patients or when endocarditis is suspected; in those groups obtain cultures regardless of chills.
ask.escalation_warning: Rigors with hypotension, altered mentation or a central line indicate probable bacteremia/sepsis: cultures, source control and antibiotics within the hour.

evidence.citation: Coburn B, Morris AM, Tomlinson G, Detsky AS. Does this adult patient with suspected bacteremia require blood cultures? JAMA. 2012;308(5):502-511.
evidence.population: Adult immunocompetent patients in whom bacteremia was suspected (35 studies; 4566 bacteremia and 25,946 negative episodes)
evidence.quote: The severity of chills graded on an ordinal scale (shaking chills, LR, 4.7; 95% CI, 3.0-7.2) may be more useful.

evidence.citation: Tokuda Y, Miyasato H, Stein GH, Kishaba T. The degree of chills for risk of bacteremia in acute febrile illness. Am J Med. 2005;118(12):1417.
evidence.population: 526 consecutive adults with acute febrile illness (40, 7.6%, bacteremic)
evidence.quote: Shaking chills showed a specificity of 90.3% (95% CI 89.2-91.5) and positive likelihood ratio of 4.65 (95% CI 2.95-6.86).
evidence.target_condition: Bacteremia - finding: shaking chills (whole-body shaking under a thick blanket)

evidence.citation: Tokuda Y, Miyasato H, Stein GH, Kishaba T. The degree of chills for risk of bacteremia in acute febrile illness. Am J Med. 2005;118(12):1417.
evidence.population: 526 consecutive adults with acute febrile illness (40, 7.6%, bacteremic)
evidence.quote: The absence of chills showed a sensitivity of 87.5% (95% CI 74.4-94.5) and negative likelihood ratio of 0.24 (95% CI 0.11-0.51).
evidence.target_condition: Bacteremia - finding: any chills (sensitivity and LR- refer to absence of chills)

ask.how: Ask the patient (or witnesses) whether they have had chills and grade the worst episode: mild = feeling cold, needing a jacket; moderate = needing a thick blanket; shaking chills = whole-body shaking even under a thick blanket. Record timing relative to fever and any line, procedure or infusion.
ask.negative_finding: Absence of any chills lowers the probability of bacteremia (LR- 0.24) but does not exclude it, particularly in elderly or immunocompromised patients who may not mount rigors.
ask.pitfalls: Rigors also occur with malaria, transfusion or drug reactions, and after amphotericin or contaminated infusions; the grading relies on patient recall and the RCE data exclude immunocompromised patients and suspected endocarditis.
ask.positive_finding: Shaking (rigor-grade) chills raise the probability of bacteremia about 4.7-fold (LR+ 4.7, 95% CI 3.0-7.2; specificity 0.90) and justify blood cultures before antibiotics.
ask.prerequisites: Patient or witness able to describe the episode; ask before antipyretics blunt recall.
ask.title: Rigors / shaking chills

ask.changes_what: Positive: de-emphasize ACS and work up PE/pneumonia/pneumothorax/pericarditis (exam, CXR, PE risk score). Negative: does not remove PE from the differential.
ask.do_not_use_when: Do not use pleuritic quality to discharge a patient with possible ACS without an ECG and troponin.
ask.escalation_warning: Pleuritic pain with hypoxemia, tachycardia, unilateral leg swelling or hemoptysis warrants immediate PE work-up; with sudden dyspnea consider pneumothorax.

evidence.citation: Panju AA, Hemmelgarn BR, Guyatt GH, Simel DL. The rational clinical examination. Is this patient having a myocardial infarction? JAMA. 1998;280(14):1256-1263.
evidence.population: Adults with acute chest pain in studies pooled by the RCE review
evidence.reference_standard: Confirmed MI by study criteria (enzymes/ECG) in included studies

evidence.citation: Courtney DM, Kline JA, Kabrhel C, et al. Clinical features from the history and physical examination that predict the presence or absence of pulmonary embolism in symptomatic emergency department patients: results of a prospective, multicenter study. Ann Emerg Med. 2010;55(4):307-315.
evidence.population: 7,940 symptomatic US ED patients tested for PE (12 centers); mean age 49, 67% female
evidence.quote: those with an adjusted odds ratio (OR) greater than 1.5 included non-cancer-related thrombophilia (OR 1.99), pleuritic chest pain (OR 1.53)
evidence.reference_standard: Imaging-confirmed PE or DVT within 45 days
evidence.target_condition: Venous thromboembolism (PE or DVT) in ED patients evaluated for PE

ask.how: Ask whether the pain is sharp and clearly worse with a deep breath, cough or sneeze (not with exertion or palpation), and whether there has been any hemoptysis. Ask separately about onset, exertional relation and positional relief so the pleuritic quality is not conflated with other descriptors.
ask.negative_finding: Absence of pleuritic quality does not exclude PE, pericarditis or pneumonia; PE frequently presents with isolated dyspnea or collapse without pleuritic pain.
ask.pitfalls: Pleuritic pain lowers but does not exclude ACS; no history element alone permits discharge without testing. Patients may label any sharp pain as breath-related unless asked specifically about inspiration.
ask.positive_finding: Pleuritic pain lowers the probability of myocardial infarction (LR about 0.2) and shifts the differential toward pulmonary embolism, pneumonia, pneumothorax, pericarditis and pleural disease. In ED patients evaluated for PE it modestly raises VTE probability (adjusted OR 1.5).
ask.prerequisites: Patient able to give a history; ask before analgesia if feasible.
ask.title: Pleuritic chest pain (sharp, worse with inspiration/cough), +/- hemoptysis

ask.changes_what: Heavy pack-year history should raise COPD/ILD on the dyspnea differential and prompt spirometry once stable; it does not discriminate the acute cause.
ask.do_not_use_when: Do not use pack-years to attribute acute dyspnea to COPD when PE, ACS, pneumothorax, or heart failure are plausible.
ask.escalation_warning: Heavy smokers with acute chest pain or dyspnea need ACS and PE considered independently of COPD history.

evidence.citation: Straus SE, McAlister FA, Sackett DL, Deeks JJ. The accuracy of patient history, wheezing, and laryngeal measurements in diagnosing obstructive airway disease. CARE-COAD1 Group. JAMA. 2000;283(14):1853-1857.
evidence.population: 309 consecutive adults at 25 primary care and referral sites in 14 countries; 25% known OAD, 37% suspected, 39% neither
evidence.quote: smoking for more than 40 pack-years (LR, 8.3), self-reported history of chronic OAD (LR, 7.3)
evidence.reference_standard: Spirometry: FEV1 and FEV1/FVC ratio < 5th percentile adjusted for height, age, sex
evidence.target_condition: Obstructive airway disease (FEV1 and FEV1/FVC below 5th percentile) - finding: smoking >40 pack-years

ask.how: Ask packs per day and years smoked; pack-years = packs/day x years (20 cigarettes = 1 pack). Record current vs former status and quit date. Thresholds studied: >40 pack-years (CARE-COAD1) and >=70 pack-years (Badgett).
ask.negative_finding: Absence of heavy smoking does not exclude airflow limitation; the LR for absence was not reported in the abstract.
ask.pitfalls: Pack-year recall is imprecise; the finding predicts chronic OAD, not whether today's dyspnea is a COPD exacerbation versus pneumonia, ACS, or PE. Heavy smoking also raises probability of ACS, lung cancer and ILD.
ask.positive_finding: >40 pack-years strongly favours obstructive airway disease (LR 8.3) in patients with known, suspected, or no OAD; with prior COPD diagnosis, >=70 pack-years plus prior diagnosis had specificity 100%.
ask.prerequisites: Reliable history from patient or informant.
ask.title: Smoking history: >40 (or >=70) pack-years, current smoker

ask.changes_what: Dysuria plus frequency without vaginal symptoms can justify empirical treatment in women; absent or nonspecific symptoms should push toward other causes of fever, AKI or delirium.
ask.do_not_use_when: The LRs apply to non-pregnant women with uncomplicated UTI; do not apply them to men, catheterized patients, or elderly patients with delirium and no new urinary symptoms.
ask.escalation_warning: Urinary symptoms with fever, rigors, flank pain, hypotension or AKI indicate pyelonephritis/urosepsis, which needs cultures, antibiotics and assessment for obstruction.

evidence.citation: Bent S, Nallamothu BK, Simel DL, Fihn SD, Saint S. Does this woman have an acute uncomplicated urinary tract infection? JAMA. 2002;287(20):2701-2710.
evidence.population: Women presenting with one or more symptoms of acute uncomplicated urinary tract infection (9 studies)
evidence.quote: dysuria (summary positive likelihood ratio [LR], 1.5; 95% confidence interval [CI], 1.2-2.0)
evidence.reference_standard: Urine culture as defined in included studies
evidence.target_condition: Acute uncomplicated urinary tract infection - finding: dysuria present

evidence.citation: Bent S, Nallamothu BK, Simel DL, Fihn SD, Saint S. Does this woman have an acute uncomplicated urinary tract infection? JAMA. 2002;287(20):2701-2710.
evidence.population: Women presenting with one or more symptoms of acute uncomplicated urinary tract infection (9 studies)
evidence.quote: absence of dysuria (summary negative LR, 0.5; 95% CI, 0.3-0.7)
evidence.reference_standard: Urine culture as defined in included studies
evidence.target_condition: Acute uncomplicated urinary tract infection - finding: dysuria absent

evidence.citation: Bent S, Nallamothu BK, Simel DL, Fihn SD, Saint S. Does this woman have an acute uncomplicated urinary tract infection? JAMA. 2002;287(20):2701-2710.
evidence.population: Women presenting with one or more symptoms of acute uncomplicated urinary tract infection (9 studies)
evidence.reference_standard: Urine culture as defined in included studies
evidence.target_condition: Acute uncomplicated urinary tract infection - finding: frequency present

evidence.citation: Bent S, Nallamothu BK, Simel DL, Fihn SD, Saint S. Does this woman have an acute uncomplicated urinary tract infection? JAMA. 2002;287(20):2701-2710.
evidence.population: Women with UTI symptoms in the single included study that examined symptom combinations
evidence.quote: 24.6 for the combination of dysuria and frequency but no vaginal discharge or irritation
evidence.reference_standard: Urine culture as defined in included studies
evidence.target_condition: Acute uncomplicated urinary tract infection - combination: dysuria and frequency without vaginal discharge or irritation

ask.how: Ask specifically about pain or burning on passing urine, new increase in frequency or urgency, and their onset; then ask about vaginal discharge or irritation, hematuria, flank pain and fever. Establish whether the symptoms are new relative to baseline (important in elderly or catheterized patients).
ask.negative_finding: Absence of dysuria lowers the probability only modestly (LR- 0.5); history alone cannot rule out UTI once one symptom is present.
ask.pitfalls: Vaginitis, urethritis and STIs mimic dysuria (vaginal discharge/irritation LR 0.2-0.3 for UTI). In elderly patients asymptomatic bacteriuria is common, and confusion without new genitourinary symptoms should not be attributed to UTI.
ask.positive_finding: In women, dysuria (LR+ 1.5) or frequency (LR+ 1.8) each raise UTI probability slightly; dysuria and frequency together without vaginal discharge or irritation raise it strongly (LR 24.6, probability above 90%).
ask.prerequisites: Patient able to give a reliable history; in delirium, obtain collateral history of new urinary symptoms.
ask.title: Dysuria and urinary frequency/urgency (new)

examine.changes_what: A positive survey targets cultures, imaging and source control (line removal, drainage, debridement); a negative survey mandates blood/urine cultures and imaging rather than reassurance.
examine.contraindications: None; do not delay cultures and antibiotics in suspected sepsis while completing the survey.
examine.do_not_use_when: Never let a negative source survey withhold cultures, empiric antibiotics or imaging in a hypotensive, febrile or acutely confused patient with suspected infection.
examine.escalation_warning: Crepitus, bullae, skin necrosis or pain out of proportion (necrotizing fasciitis), a hot joint, peritonism, or purulence at a central line/dialysis catheter in a septic patient require immediate surgical/source-control and line removal decisions.
examine.how: Undress and inspect every line, dialysis and drain/exit site (erythema, purulence, tunnel tenderness), all skin including back, sacrum, heels, perineum, injection sites and wounds; palpate abdomen (peritonism, Murphy sign, flank tenderness), joints and spine for warmth/effusion/tenderness; check urinary catheter, mouth, sinuses, ears and chest. Repeat daily while the source is unknown.
examine.negative_finding: A normal survey does not exclude an occult source: insertion-site inflammation is absent in nearly all catheter-related bloodstream infections, and intra-abdominal, urinary, endovascular and spinal infections are frequently silent in elderly, immunosuppressed or sedated patients.
examine.pitfalls: Line-site appearance has near-zero sensitivity for CRBSI (coagulase-negative staphylococci cause little inflammation); steroids, neutropenia and neuropathy blunt local signs; dressings, obesity and immobility hide sacral, perineal and injection-site infections. Pain out of proportion with unimpressive skin findings suggests necrotizing infection.
examine.positive_finding: Purulence, spreading erythema or tunnel tenderness at a line/exit site, cellulitis or crepitus, a hot swollen joint, peritonism or flank tenderness, or a sacral/heel ulcer with surrounding infection identifies a probable source and directs cultures, source control and empiric therapy.
examine.prerequisites: Full exposure with dressings taken down, adequate lighting and analgesia; review lines, catheters and devices with their insertion dates; log-roll immobile patients to view the sacrum.
examine.title: Focused infection-source exam (line/exit sites, skin, abdomen, joints, sacrum, urine catheter)

examine.changes_what: RR >24 with fever/cough: image for pneumonia and assess severity. Normal vitals in low-risk cough: CXR may be deferred. Unexplained tachypnea: check gas/lactate for acidosis.
examine.do_not_use_when: Do not use a normal RR to exclude PE, sepsis or acidosis; do not rely on charted (estimated) rates.
examine.escalation_warning: RR >=30, or RR >=22 with altered mentation or SBP <=100 (qSOFA >=2), or tachypnea with rising PCO2/fatigue: escalate to higher level of care.

evidence.citation: Htun TP, Sun Y, Chua HL, Pang J. Clinical features for diagnosis of pneumonia among adults in primary care setting: A systematic and meta-review. Sci Rep. 2019;9:7600.
evidence.location: Table 2 (PMC6527561 full text); footnote ¥ gives thresholds
evidence.population: Adults with respiratory symptoms in primary care, no serious illness; 6 studies, n=4,468
evidence.target_condition: Radiographic community-acquired pneumonia (respiratory rate >=20/min; >=22 in one study, >=24 in two)

evidence.citation: Ebell MH, Chupp H, Cai X, Bentivegna M, Kearney M. Accuracy of Signs and Symptoms for the Diagnosis of Community-acquired Pneumonia: A Meta-analysis. Acad Emerg Med. 2020;27(7):541-553.
evidence.population: Adults with suspected pneumonia or acute cough; 17 prospective cohorts (9 primary care, 7 ED)
evidence.quote: it is decreased most by the absence of abnormal vital signs (LR- = 0.25, 95% CI = 0.11 to 0.48)
evidence.target_condition: Community-acquired pneumonia (absence of ANY abnormal vital sign, composite including respiratory rate)

examine.how: Count chest-wall excursions for a full 60 seconds while the patient is at rest and unaware (e.g., while appearing to take the pulse). Do not use the triage estimate or a 15-second count multiplied; record the pattern (deep Kussmaul vs shallow rapid) as well as the rate.
examine.negative_finding: A normal rate lowers but does not exclude pneumonia (LR- 0.77); absence of any vital-sign abnormality lowers CAP probability more strongly (LR- 0.25).
examine.pitfalls: Recorded rates are often estimated rather than counted, clustering at 18-20. Pain, anxiety, fever and hypoxia raise the rate nonspecifically; PE frequently presents with RR >20 but the finding is not discriminating.
examine.positive_finding: RR above threshold raises the probability of radiographic pneumonia (pooled LR+ 3.5 for RR >=20-24) and is a qSOFA/CURB-65 criterion; deep regular tachypnea points to metabolic acidosis or uremia.
examine.prerequisites: Patient at rest for several minutes; not talking.
examine.title: Respiratory rate >24-25/min counted for 60 s

examine.changes_what: Diffuse wheeze: treat airflow limitation and confirm with spirometry/peak flow; new wheeze with edema/JVP elevation should prompt evaluation for heart failure rather than bronchodilators alone.
examine.contraindications: None, but avoid repeated forced expirations in a patient near exhaustion.
examine.do_not_use_when: Do not use absence of wheeze to exclude severe asthma or COPD exacerbation, or to exclude heart failure or pulmonary embolism as the cause of dyspnea.
examine.escalation_warning: Silent chest, inability to speak, drowsiness or stridor with wheeze (possible anaphylaxis or upper-airway obstruction) requires immediate airway and resuscitation measures.

evidence.citation: Straus SE, McAlister FA, Sackett DL, Deeks JJ; CARE-COAD1 Group. The accuracy of patient history, wheezing, and laryngeal measurements in diagnosing obstructive airway disease. JAMA. 2000;283(14):1853-1857.
evidence.population: 309 consecutive patients at 25 primary care and referral sites in 14 countries (25% known, 37% suspected OAD); 52% had OAD
evidence.quote: The LR for wheezing was 2.7 (95% confidence interval [CI], 1.7-4.2)
evidence.reference_standard: Spirometry: FEV1 and FEV1/FVC below 5th percentile adjusted for height, age and sex

evidence.citation: Arts L, Lim EHT, van de Ven PM, Heunks L, Tuinman PR. The diagnostic accuracy of lung auscultation in adult patients with acute pulmonary pathologies: a meta-analysis. Sci Rep. 2020;10:7347.
evidence.population: Adults with known or suspected COPD/asthma, 10 studies

evidence.citation: Arts L, Lim EHT, van de Ven PM, Heunks L, Tuinman PR. The diagnostic accuracy of lung auscultation in adult patients with acute pulmonary pathologies: a meta-analysis. Sci Rep. 2020;10:7347.
evidence.reference_standard: Doppler echocardiography, Framingham criteria or expert panel
evidence.target_condition: Congestive heart failure (cardiogenic pulmonary edema) - wheezes

examine.how: Auscultate all lung fields during tidal breathing and then during a forced expiration, noting whether wheeze is diffuse and polyphonic (airflow limitation) or focal and monophonic (localized obstruction). Listen over the neck to separate inspiratory stridor from expiratory wheeze.
examine.negative_finding: No wheeze does not exclude airflow limitation (sensitivity roughly 0.25-0.3); a 'silent chest' in a distressed asthmatic indicates critically low airflow, not improvement.
examine.pitfalls: Wheeze occurs in heart failure ('cardiac asthma') and pneumonia and does not discriminate them; its intensity does not track severity. Sensitivity is low and pooled specificity for obstructive disease around 0.9.
examine.positive_finding: Diffuse polyphonic expiratory wheeze supports airflow limitation (asthma/COPD); a fixed focal monophonic wheeze suggests localized bronchial obstruction; predominantly inspiratory noise over the neck is stridor.
examine.prerequisites: Patient able to take deep and forced breaths; quiet setting.
examine.title: Wheezing on auscultation (diffuse expiratory vs focal/monophonic)

examine.changes_what: Focal egophony in a febrile, coughing patient raises pneumonia probability substantially (LR+ about 6); proceed to CXR/LUS and empiric treatment as clinically indicated.
examine.do_not_use_when: Do not use absence of egophony to withhold imaging in a patient with hypoxia, abnormal vital signs or immunocompromise.
examine.escalation_warning: Egophony plus hypotension, RR >30 or confusion suggests severe pneumonia; assess for sepsis and consider admission.

evidence.citation: Ebell MH, Chupp H, Cai X, Bentivegna M, Kearney M. Accuracy of signs and symptoms for the diagnosis of community-acquired pneumonia: a meta-analysis. Acad Emerg Med. 2020;27(7):541-553.
evidence.population: Adults with clinically suspected pneumonia or acute cough; 17 prospective cohorts (9 primary care, 7 ED); CAP prevalence 10% primary care, 20% ED

examine.how: Auscultate the posterior and lateral chest while the patient repeatedly says a sustained 'ee'; egophony is present where the sound is heard as a nasal 'ay' (A) over a focal area but as 'ee' elsewhere. Compare with breath sounds at the same site for a harsh, tubular bronchial quality with a pause between inspiration and expiration.
examine.negative_finding: Normal vesicular sounds and 'ee' transmitted unchanged; absence has little rule-out value because the sign is insensitive.
examine.pitfalls: Sensitivity is low so most pneumonias lack egophony; it also occurs over the compressed lung at the upper border of a pleural effusion and can be mimicked at the trachea and interscapular area in thin patients.
examine.positive_finding: Focal E-to-A change and/or bronchial breath sounds over lung parenchyma, indicating consolidation or the compressed lung above an effusion.
examine.prerequisites: Cooperative patient able to phonate; compare with the contralateral side at the same level.
examine.title: Egophony (E-to-A change) or bronchial breath sounds over a focal area
